column1: # Computing, internet and digital-finance vocabulary newer than WordNet 3.0
# (2006), and the IT abbreviations a reader of technical material meets.
#   word <TAB> part of speech <TAB> definition <TAB> alias|alias…
# Merged into the general English dictionary, after any WordNet senses.

column3: A shared digital ledger in which records are grouped into blocks, each linked to the one before by a cryptographic hash, so that past entries cannot be altered without detection.
The first and largest cryptocurrency, launched in 2009; transactions are recorded on a public blockchain and no central authority issues it.
A digital currency that uses cryptography to secure transactions and control the creation of new units, usually recorded on a blockchain.
A public blockchain platform that runs smart contracts; its currency is ether (ETH).
A cryptocurrency designed to hold a steady value by being tied to a currency or other asset.
Financial technology: the use of software and digital platforms to deliver financial services; also a company that does so.
Distributed Ledger Technology: a database shared and synchronised across many computers with no central administrator; blockchain is one kind.
Software written to damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access to a computer system; includes viruses, worms, trojans and ransomware.
Malware that encrypts a victim's files or locks a system and demands payment to restore access.
Tricking people into revealing passwords or card details through messages or websites that imitate a trusted organisation.
Software that secretly gathers information about a user's activity and sends it to someone else.
A network of infected computers controlled remotely, typically used to send spam or launch attacks.
Relating to computers, networks and the internet: cyber attack, cyber law.
The protection of computers, networks and data from unauthorised access, attack or damage.
An attempt to damage, disrupt or break into a computer system or network.
Crime committed using computers or the internet.
Software that detects and removes malware.
Using a person's physical characteristics — fingerprint, face, iris, voice — to confirm identity.
A mobile phone with a touchscreen, internet access and the ability to run apps.
An application: a program built for a particular task, especially one for a phone or tablet.
The act of signing in to a system by proving identity; also the credentials used.
The act of ending a signed-in session.
The name that identifies a user to a system, entered together with a password.
The folder where incoming email or messages arrive.
Not connected to a network or the internet; done without such a connection.
A private network that gives selected outsiders — partners, suppliers, customers — controlled access to part of an organisation's intranet.
A single document on the World Wide Web, shown in a browser.
A file of rules, usually CSS, that defines how a web page looks.
A display that detects the touch of a finger or stylus and uses it as input.
A record of the date and time at which an event happened or data was created.
A person or program that checks something is valid; in a blockchain, a participant that verifies transactions and adds blocks.
Able to be given instructions to perform a task automatically.
The capacity to be programmed.
Taking place between banks: interbank transfer, interbank rate.
Working without physical contact: a contactless card pays when held near the reader.
Small loans, savings and other financial services for people with low incomes who lack access to ordinary banking.
Creating virtual versions of computers, storage or networks so that several can run on one physical machine.
A program that holds a conversation with people in text or speech.
A website or page of regularly updated posts, usually by one author.
A series of spoken audio episodes distributed over the internet.
A website whose pages its users can edit together.
A small picture used in digital messages to express an idea or feeling.
A word or phrase preceded by # that labels a social-media post by topic.
Floating-point operations per second: a measure of computer speed. A petaFLOPS is 10^15 and an exaFLOPS 10^18 per second.
The programming language that runs in web browsers and makes pages interactive; also used on servers.
The fifth major version of HTML, adding native audio, video, graphics and richer forms.
Cascading Style Sheets: the language that describes the presentation — layout, colours, fonts — of a web page.
A widely used open-source relational database management system.
Database systems that store data in forms other than relational tables, such as documents or key–value pairs.
Application Programming Interface: a defined way for one program to request services from another.
Software Development Kit: tools and libraries for building software for a particular platform.
Integrated Development Environment: one program combining an editor, build tools and a debugger.
Internet Service Provider: a company that connects customers to the internet.
Virtual Private Network: an encrypted connection over a public network that behaves like a private one.
Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure: HTTP carried over an encrypted TLS connection, so that data between browser and website cannot be read or altered.
Hypertext Transfer Protocol: the rules by which browsers request pages from web servers.
Secure Sockets Layer: the earlier protocol for encrypting internet connections, now replaced by TLS.
Transport Layer Security: the protocol that encrypts data travelling between two computers; the basis of HTTPS.
Internet Message Access Protocol: lets a mail program read email that stays stored on the server, in step across devices.
Post Office Protocol version 3: downloads email from a server to one device, usually removing it from the server.
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: the protocol used to send email between servers.
File Transfer Protocol: a standard way of moving files between computers on a network.
Domain Name System: translates names such as example.com into the numeric IP addresses computers use.
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol: automatically gives devices on a network an IP address and settings.
Transmission Control Protocol: delivers data between computers reliably and in order.
User Datagram Protocol: sends data quickly without guaranteeing delivery or order.
Internet Protocol: the addressing and routing rules of the internet. An IP address identifies a device on a network.
Local Area Network: a network covering one building or site.
Wide Area Network: a network spanning cities or countries.
Metropolitan Area Network: a network covering a city.
Uniform Resource Locator: the address of a page or file on the web.
Central Processing Unit: the part of a computer that carries out instructions; its processor.
Graphics Processing Unit: a processor built for images and for large parallel calculations.
Random-Access Memory: a computer's fast working memory, cleared when power is lost.
Read-Only Memory: memory whose contents are kept without power and are not normally changed.
Solid-State Drive: storage using flash memory with no moving parts; faster than a hard disk.
Hard Disk Drive: storage that records data on spinning magnetic disks.
Universal Serial Bus: the standard connector and protocol for attaching devices to a computer.
Basic Input/Output System: firmware that starts a computer's hardware before the operating system loads.
Graphical User Interface: windows, icons and menus operated with a pointer or touch.
Command-Line Interface: operating a computer by typing commands.
Operating System: the software that manages a computer's hardware and runs its programs.
Database Management System: software for creating, querying and maintaining databases.
Structured Query Language: the standard language for querying and changing relational databases.
Enterprise Resource Planning: integrated software running an organisation's core processes — finance, stock, payroll.
Customer Relationship Management: software and practices for managing dealings with customers.
Internet of Things: everyday devices fitted with sensors and network connections so they can exchange data.
Artificial Intelligence: computer systems that perform tasks normally needing human intelligence.
Machine Learning: methods by which computers improve at a task by finding patterns in data.
Uninterruptible Power Supply: a battery unit that keeps equipment running briefly when mains power fails.
Nepal Telecommunications Authority: the regulator of telecommunications in Nepal.
United States dollar.
An American technology company, maker of Windows, Office and the Azure cloud platform.
Google's email service.
